scenes.title: Start in the department Records Settings

captions.text: Record numbers help people find and distinguish documents during
a handover or a data migration.
This walkthrough starts on Records Settings in the fictional Firehouse
fifty-one training department.
We will inspect the numbering controls, save one change, verify what persisted
and restore the original pattern.
The department name and settings page should match the department
you intend to administer.

scenes.title: Read the number pattern and its tokens

captions.text: Scroll to Record numbering.
Number pattern currently contains the prefix token, a hyphen, the
four-digit year token, another hyphen and the sequence token.
The help below explains what each token writes.
Prefix uses the record type prefix, year includes the numbering year,
and sequence supplies the counter.
Changing this pattern does not renumber records that already have numbers.
Read that impact before applying a new format.

scenes.title: Distinguish padding from the next sequence

captions.text: Sequence digits is four in this department.
The help shows that four digits writes a zero-padded value
such as zero one eight four.
This control accepts three through eight digits.
Changing the width keeps each sequence's next number; it is not the same as
choosing a different next counter.
Definitions that have their own numbering keep their own width.
In this exercise, we leave the four-digit setting as it is.
Numbering year starts has a month and day.
January first is selected here.
The displayed help explains how a fiscal-year start affects
sequences that include the year.
This setting is separate from call numbering, which has its
own year start on Call Settings.
Review the policy your department actually follows before changing either.
This demonstration keeps the existing January-first value.

scenes.title: Understand type prefixes and shared sequences

captions.text: Record type prefixes lists each type, its default and a Number prefix box.
The visible defaults include Run, R U N; Training, T R N;
Work, W R K; and Meeting, M T G.
Leave a box blank to keep its default.
The help explains that a new prefix starts its own sequence, and types given
the same prefix share one sequence.
Prefixes take effect when the number pattern includes the prefix token.
Choose them deliberately rather than using a cosmetic change that
accidentally joins two counters.

scenes.title: Prepare a custom pattern in the training department

captions.text: For this local exercise, replace the two hyphens in Number
pattern with underscores.
Keep the same prefix, four-digit year and sequence tokens.

spoken_references.{PREFIX}_{YYYY}_{SEQ}: prefix, four-digit year and sequence tokens

captions.text: The example beside the field now uses underscores too.
This is still an unsaved form value.
The format of the example is useful feedback, but it does not prove
the department has saved the change or issued a new record number.
Scroll to the bottom of Records Settings, where Save and Cancel are visible.
Review your intended edit before choosing Save.
This demonstration changes the number pattern only; it does not submit a
record, raise a counter or request delivery to an external service.
Use Save once, then verify the returned settings page instead
of assuming that typing in the field completed the configuration.
The returned page displays Records settings saved.
This confirms that the settings form was accepted.
We still need to verify the particular value we intended to change.
A general success notice is useful, but reading the saved
field and its effect gives an administrator a more complete check.
Reopening Records Settings shows the underscore-separated pattern
in Number pattern, with the matching example alongside it.
This is a fresh page load after saving.
Compare the full pattern, including each token and separator,
with your intended format.
The result confirms persistence of this local setting; the example is still an
example rather than a newly issued record.

scenes.title: Inspect the effect on next-number previews

captions.text: The saved pattern changes Next numbers for twenty twenty-six.
The Run and Training previews now have underscores and end in zero zero zero one.
The text around the sequence token changed, so this
format has its own sequence.
Raise next to is a separate control for carrying on from
previously issued numbers.
Leave it alone when you do not intend to raise a counter.
Viewing this table does not issue the previewed numbers.

scenes.title: Restore the original pattern for the exercise

captions.text: After the exercise, the original hyphen-separated pattern was restored.
Record numbering now shows the original prefix, year and sequence arrangement.
Restore a practice change only when that is your intended configuration.
Changing separators back is a format decision; it is not a
way to erase previously issued numbers or reset a counter.
The original format now shows Training ending in zero zero zero

spoken_references.TRN-2026-0003: Training ending in zero zero zero

captions.text: three, the same next-number preview it had before the demonstration.
Run ends in zero zero zero one.

spoken_references.RUN-2026-0001: Run ends in zero zero zero one

captions.text: Restoring the earlier format resumed its existing sequence rather
than restarting Training at one.
No new records were issued during this exercise.
When importing from another system, review Raise next to against the
numbers already issued before applying a higher starting point.
Other record numbers has separate rows for Records requests, Occupancies,
Inspections, Permits and Investigations.
Each visible row has a Number pattern, Sequence digits and a next-number area.
The help explains that blank patterns keep the built-in numbers
and that these types follow the record-numbering year start above.
Review the particular row you intend to administer.
This recording inspects those controls without saving a custom
pattern for these other record types.

scenes.title: Apply a clear numbering policy across departments

captions.text: A consistent numbering policy helps security teams find post reports,
wildland contractors distinguish crew-support work, and industrial
teams coordinate equipment records.
Community paramedicine and mental health teams can organize appropriate
service documentation, while search-and-rescue teams can distinguish
training and support records.
Fire and E M S departments can use the same pattern review.
Agree on the format, inspect the correct controls, save deliberately
and verify both persistence and the next-number preview.
